title: Behavioral > Self-Reported Evidence
intro: When the question is usability, the best evidence comes from observing behaviour. The closer you get to real tasks, real constraints and real consequences, the more trustworthy the data.

learn.title: Three categories, not two
learn.text:
**Behavioural evidence** — task completion or failure, critical errors and where they happen, backtracking and hesitation, time on task when meaningful, moments where the user needs help, accessibility outcomes like keyboard operability.

**Perception evidence** — what the participant believed the system was doing, what they thought a control meant, what goal they were pursuing, what felt missing, what they expected next.

**Sentiment** — “I liked it”, “it feels modern”, “it was intuitive”, ratings and NPS-style prompts.

try.q: A participant says they thought the “Archive” button would delete the item. Which category is that?
try.explain: What they believed the system was doing — valuable, but not a record of what happened.

right.label: Perception and sentiment
items: What they thought a control meant

learn.title: The rule of thumb
learn.text:
**If behavioural evidence and perception evidence conflict, behavioural evidence wins.**

That doesn't mean ignoring what the person said. It means interpreting the statement in light of what they did — the quote explains the behaviour, it doesn't override it.

A quote from a discovery interview, a post-task rating and a screen recording of task failure are all data. Treating them as interchangeable is the mistake.

try.q: A user rates the task 4/5 for ease but failed it twice on video. Which do you lead with?
try.explain: Behavioural evidence wins; the rating then helps explain why they felt it went well.

learn.title: Why teams get this wrong
learn.text:
Three predictable reasons, and none of them is that users lie:

**1. Perception data is easy to package.** A clean quote looks good on a slide and travels well through an organisation.

**2. It often aligns with what stakeholders already want to be true.** Confirmation bias turns a single quote into a decision.

**3. Lean UX culture trained teams to over-index on lightweight discovery.** Interview-driven discovery crowds out observation — the reason that annoys Calabro most, because the HCI field is not new.

try.q: Why does perception data travel so well in organisations?
options: A clean quote packages easily for a slide
try.explain: Easy to package, and it often matches what people already believe.

test.q: What is the rule of thumb when the two kinds of evidence conflict?
test.explain: You still interpret the statement — you just don't let it override what happened.

test.q: Which of these is behavioural evidence?
options: What the user expected to happen
test.explain: Along with completion, errors, time on task and accessibility outcomes.

options: Lean UX over-indexing on lightweight discovery
Survey tools being too easy to use
test.explain: Because the HCI field is not new — this was settled decades ago.

test.q: What makes evidence more trustworthy, according to the opening?
options: Real tasks, real constraints, real consequences
A larger and more diverse sample
test.explain: The closer you get to those, the better the data.

test.q: What is wrong with treating a quote, a rating and a screen recording as the same thing?
options: Quotes are less reliable than ratings
test.explain: All three are data; the error is interchangeability.
